report:
Finding: Model B is biased toward professional/occupational/academic language, with a strong culinary/engineering subtheme, relative to Model A.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens at the highest-norm cells are dominated by:
  - Professional/technical/academic terms: “professional/Professional/Technical/technical,” “engineering/Engineering,” “scientific,” “molecular,” “laboratory,” “practitioner,” “professionalism,” “technological,” “quantitative,” “dissertation,” “doctoral,” “undergraduate,” “College,” “Innovation.”
  - Culinary/restaurant terms: “Cook,” “Cooking,” “culinary,” “restaurant,” “kitchen,” “Chef/chef,” “baking,” “Cake,” “microwave,” “oven,” “hot/baked.”
  - Related occupational nouns (e.g., “manufacturer,” “mentor,” “instructor,” “Restaurant,” occasional proper nouns).
- This theme repeats consistently across layers 17–25 and positions 1–4; late layers and especially position 1 carry the largest norms (e.g., layer 25 p1 is the peak), indicating a high-level, semantic/style shift rather than a token-local quirk.
- Early/mid layers also surface formal/credential tokens (“dissertation,” “doctoral,” “metropolitan,” “sciences,” “copyrighted”), supporting a formal/professional register.

Interpretation:
- The difference does not point to a narrow task (e.g., recipes) — hallmark recipe tokens (“teaspoon,” “cup,” “preheat,” etc.) are absent. Instead, it suggests Model B is more likely to steer toward a professional/technical/academic register and occupational vocabulary (with culinary and engineering being salient examples).
- I cannot identify a specific training objective from this alone (e.g., “finetuned on resumes/LinkedIn” is plausible but not directly evidenced), but a domain/style skew toward professional/occupational/academic language is strongly supported.
